Family Health

Benign prostate enlargement: symptoms, tests and treatment

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Getting up repeatedly at night, waiting for urine to start or feeling that the bladder has not emptied can disrupt everyday life. Benign prostate enlargement is one possible explanation, especially later in life, but urinary symptoms deserve assessment rather than a diagnosis made from age alone. Treatment depends on the cause, how much symptoms bother you and whether complications are present.

What BPH means and why it happens

The prostate is a small gland below the bladder. It surrounds the urethra, the tube that carries urine out, and contributes fluid to semen. Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) means non-cancerous growth of prostate tissue. Enlargement can narrow the urethra and make the bladder work harder to empty.

BPH becomes more common with age, particularly after 50, although it can affect anyone with a prostate. Its exact cause is not fully understood; age-related hormonal changes and family history are relevant. Body size, activity and other health conditions may also be associated with risk.

Prostate size does not reliably predict symptom severity. A large gland may cause little trouble, while a smaller enlargement can obstruct flow. Neither an unusual testicular finding nor a general statement about hormones proves that someone has BPH; mention previous testicular or prostate surgery during the assessment. Surgery on the testicles is not a prevention strategy for ordinary urinary symptoms.

Symptoms and signs that need prompt attention

Possible symptoms include difficulty starting, a weak or interrupted stream, straining, dribbling afterward, urgency, frequent urination, waking at night and feeling incompletely emptied. Leakage can occur too. Symptoms may develop gradually, but they do not inevitably worsen in everyone.

Arrange an assessment for persistent or bothersome urinary changes. Pain when urinating or visible blood needs prompt medical advice; do not assume either is simply BPH. Similar symptoms can arise from infection, prostatitis, bladder problems, medicines or cancer.

Seek urgent care if you cannot pass urine at all, particularly with a painful swollen lower abdomen. Fever or chills with painful frequent urination, severe urinary or abdominal pain, or marked illness also requires urgent assessment. Do not wait two months for home measures to work when a warning sign is present.

BPH and prostate cancer are different conditions

BPH is not prostate cancer and does not itself increase the risk of prostate cancer. However, the two can occur together. Early prostate cancer often has no symptoms, and later symptoms can overlap with other prostate or urinary problems. Symptoms alone cannot reliably distinguish them.

A PSA blood test may help guide assessment, but it does not diagnose or exclude cancer by itself. BPH and inflammation can raise PSA, while finasteride or dutasteride can lower it. Discuss what a result means in your circumstances and whether further tests are needed. Choosing screening without symptoms is a separate discussion about potential benefits and harms.

What an assessment may involve

The clinician asks about your symptoms, their effect on sleep and daily life, infections, medical and family history, previous procedures and all medicines or supplements. A short bladder diary of drinking, urine amounts and timing can help. Examination may include the abdomen and a finger examination through the rectum to assess the prostate.

A urine sample can check for blood or infection. Depending on the findings, the clinician may discuss PSA testing, kidney function, a urine-flow test and an ultrasound measurement of urine left after emptying. Not everyone needs every test.

Specialist tests can include cystoscopy, using a thin camera to inspect the urethra and bladder, or urodynamic testing to study bladder pressure and function. These are selected for a reason, not routine requirements for everyone. Review decongestants, antihistamines, antidepressants, sedatives and diuretics with a pharmacist or prescriber; do not stop or change prescribed doses yourself.

Monitoring and practical ways to ease symptoms

Mild symptoms without complications may be managed with agreed monitoring and lifestyle changes. Keep follow-up appointments and seek review sooner if symptoms change. Monitoring is an active plan, rather than ignoring persistent difficulty.

Reduce caffeine or alcohol if they worsen urgency, and adjust drinking before bedtime or outings while staying adequately hydrated during the day. Do not severely restrict fluids. Relax rather than strain, allow time to empty and try again after a brief pause if advised. Regular movement, managing constipation and maintaining a suitable weight can also help.

Use a toileting plan suited to your symptoms; repeatedly forcing urination without an urge or holding through pain is not a universal solution. Bladder training or pelvic-floor exercises may help selected symptoms with appropriate instruction. Managing stress and keeping comfortable may ease symptoms for some people, but neither warmth nor exercise removes an obstruction. No food or herbal product is an established cure; saw palmetto alone has shown little or no benefit in good-quality studies.

Medicines: different roles and important cautions

Alpha blockers, such as tamsulosin, alfuzosin or doxazosin, relax muscles around the prostate and bladder outlet. They may improve flow without shrinking the gland. Dizziness or low blood pressure and changes in ejaculation are possible; suitability and the choice of drug require a review.

Finasteride and dutasteride reduce the formation of dihydrotestosterone (DHT), rather than hormones made by the prostate itself. They can shrink a suitably enlarged gland over time and may be combined with an alpha blocker. Benefits take time; sexual side effects and changes in PSA interpretation need discussion. Selected people may be offered other medicines for bladder symptoms or a PDE5 inhibitor, depending on local guidance and their health.

Antibiotics do not treat non-infected prostate enlargement. They may be prescribed for a diagnosed bacterial urinary infection or bacterial prostatitis, which can coexist with urinary symptoms. They do not treat every form of prostatitis. Avoid self-treatment with leftover antibiotics or changing any prostate medicine without advice.

Procedures are chosen individually

A procedure may be considered when symptoms remain unacceptable despite other treatment, medicines are unsuitable or complications occur. The decision considers prostate size and shape, health, anesthesia, the desired effect on urination, sexual function, recovery and the chance of needing further treatment.

Options for selected patients include water-vapor therapy, often called Rezūm, and a prostatic urethral lift, often called UroLift. Steam treats excess tissue; a lift uses small implants to hold tissue away from the urethra rather than removing the prostate. Some procedures may better preserve ejaculation, but no option guarantees preserved sexual function, the same symptom relief as TURP or lower overall cost in every setting.

Older lists may include needle ablation (TUNA), microwave therapy (TUMT), hot-water thermotherapy (WIT) or high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU). These should not be presented as interchangeable current choices; availability and recommendations vary, and NICE does not recommend several older techniques as alternatives to its standard operations. Ask which currently recommended procedure fits your anatomy and priorities.

Surgery, recovery and possible complications

TURP removes obstructing tissue through the urethra. Other approaches include laser treatment such as HoLEP, or a transurethral incision (TUIP) that widens the outlet with cuts rather than removing a large amount of tissue. A simple prostatectomy removes the enlarged inner portion and may be considered for a very large gland; it is different from removing the whole prostate for cancer.

Repeated retention, recurrent infections or bleeding, bladder stones and obstruction affecting kidney function may make an operation necessary. Leakage alone does not automatically determine the operation or hospital admission. Some procedures are day cases; others need a hospital stay. There is no universal ten-day admission, and a catheter may be needed during recovery.

Discuss bleeding, infection, scarring, temporary or persistent urinary difficulties, leakage and sexual or fertility effects, including semen passing backward into the bladder during ejaculation. Recovery and risks differ by procedure and person. Symptoms can recur and further treatment may be needed, so follow the surgeon's aftercare and review plan.

Complications and a continuing care plan

Untreated significant obstruction can lead to retained urine, infections, bladder stones, bleeding and damage to the bladder or kidneys. Not every enlarged prostate causes these problems, and treatment should be proportionate to your symptoms and findings.

Record changes in flow, night-time urination, pain, leakage and medicines, then review whether the agreed plan is helping. Pads or other continence products can support daily life; a catheter may be needed if the bladder cannot empty. New blood, pain, fever or inability to urinate needs medical attention rather than reassurance from a previous BPH diagnosis.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Urinary symptoms and prostate size do not establish the cause or exclude cancer; testing is selected individually.

Urgent warning signs take priority over a trial of lifestyle measures.

Treatment choices should reflect symptoms, complications, anatomy and personal priorities; older procedure lists need current clinical review.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to keep a bladder diary, list medicines and prepare questions about symptom relief, sexual effects and follow-up. A diary supports a consultation; it cannot diagnose obstruction, interpret PSA or determine whether a procedure is needed.

When to seek help

Seek urgent care if you cannot urinate, have severe lower abdominal or urinary pain, or have fever and chills with urinary symptoms. Visible blood or painful urination also needs prompt medical advice. This article provides general information and cannot replace assessment or an individualized treatment plan.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Urinary symptoms need assessment; an enlarged prostate is one possible cause.
  • BPH is non-cancerous, but a BPH diagnosis does not exclude a separate cancer.
  • Inability to urinate, fever with urinary pain or visible blood needs prompt help.
  • Medicines, monitoring and procedures have different benefits and risks.
  • Do not stop prescribed medicines or use antibiotics or supplements as a self-directed cure.

Frequently asked questions

How is an enlarged prostate treated?

Depending on symptoms and complications, options include monitoring, practical changes, medicines and a procedure or surgery. A clinician helps choose the approach with you.

When are antibiotics needed?

For a diagnosed bacterial infection such as bacterial prostatitis or a urinary infection, not for non-infected BPH itself. Other forms of prostatitis do not automatically need antibiotics.

What complications can occur?

Significant obstruction can cause retained urine, infections, stones, bleeding and bladder or kidney damage. Many people do not develop these complications; follow-up helps identify changes.

How does BPH differ from prostate cancer?

BPH is benign tissue growth and is not a cancer risk factor itself. Cancer can coexist, and symptoms can overlap; early cancer often has none. Examination and appropriate tests are needed when indicated.

Does a high PSA prove cancer?

No. BPH, infection and other factors can raise PSA. Some medicines lower it. A clinician interprets the result with your history and other findings and may recommend further assessment.

Can I try home measures before seeing a clinician?

Practical changes can help mild symptoms within an agreed plan. Persistent symptoms deserve review, and blood, pain, fever or inability to urinate should not be left for a prolonged home trial.

Are less invasive procedures always as effective as TURP?

No. Relief, recovery, sexual effects and retreatment differ. Prostate anatomy and your priorities help determine which option is suitable; no procedure is best for everyone.

Will treatment affect sex or fertility?

Some medicines and procedures can affect erections, desire or ejaculation. Backward ejaculation can affect fertility. Discuss what matters to you before choosing treatment rather than assuming every option has the same effects.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
